stemBlocks.value: A = (1 2 / 0 3) and B = (4 −1 / 2 5). (a) Calculate AB. (b) Calculate BA. (c) Hence show that matrix multiplication is not commutative for A and B.
Think first: You must do the two multiplications separately — the order of the letters changes which rows meet which columns.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p199-q11 from workbook page 199.

solutionSteps.instruction: Multiply the rows of A into the columns of B.
Now multiply the rows of B into the columns of A.

contentBlocks.value: 8 ≠ 4 in the top-left position alone is enough.

strategyBlocks.value: Compute AB with rows of A into columns of B, compute BA with rows of B into columns of A, then compare the two results entry by entry.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) AB = (8 9 / 6 15)  (b) BA = (4 5 / 2 19)  (c) The two products differ — for example the entry in row 1, column 1 is 8 in AB but 4 in BA — so AB ≠ BA and matrix multiplication is not commutative for these matrices.

whyThisWorks.value: In a product, the first matrix supplies the rows and the second supplies the columns, so swapping the letters changes every pairing. That is why AB and BA are generally different matrices even when both are defined and the same size. One mismatched entry is all that is needed to prove non-commutativity.
